genesis_measure.py.notes:
The results of this indicate a bias which is not good: 20 runs. Every single angle between 1.02 and 1.96. Standard deviation 0.218 on a range of 0 to 6.28. The system is consistently picking the same direction.

This is not spontaneous symmetry breaking. There's a bias in the system that prefers angles near θ ≈ 1.4 (roughly π/4 ≈ 0.785 to π/2 ≈ 1.57). That's the diagonal direction of the square grid.

The ordering is real — |m| is consistently around 0.32, the system does organize. But it's the square lattice doing the symmetry breaking, not the field dynamics. The 4-neighbor coupling on a square grid with forward-difference derivatives in the compression rule creates a preferred axis along the grid diagonal.

This is an important and honest result. It means:

The system does order (|m| >> 0)
But the direction is set by the lattice geometry, not chosen spontaneously
The "SSB" we were celebrating was actually explicit breaking by the square grid topology
What would fix this and produce a real test:

Hexagonal lattice — 6 neighbors instead of 4, higher rotational symmetry. If the bias disappears, it was the square grid.
Symmetric finite differences — the compression rule uses forward differences (roll(-1) - self) which are asymmetric. Central differences ((roll(-1) - roll(+1)) / 2) would remove that directional bias.
Random neighbor topology — Voronoi or Delaunay mesh instead of a regular grid. No preferred directions at all.
The simplest fix to try first: switch the compression rule's finite differences from forward to central. That might eliminate the bias without changing the lattice.
